title: Mary in Carmel
hook: an order that calls Mary both mother and sister

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Compiègne offering, a convent's lives given for peace long before the scaffold. Your line was an offering for peace. Which tedious part of the day did you hand over? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

Families have their own names for the people they love. Mom, Nana, Auntie, Sis. The Carmelites carry Mary in their very name: they are the brothers and sisters of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel. But inside the order, people speak of her in two ways that don't usually go together. She is their mother. And she is their sister. One person, two names, two kinds of closeness. Today, Mary in Carmel.
screen: `A FAMILY'S NAMES.` → `MARY IN THE ORDER'S NAME.` → `MOTHER, AND SISTER.`

segments.voice: First, mother. At the cross, John's Gospel says, Jesus looks at his mother and at the disciple he loves, and gives them to each other. In the Douay-Rheims: "After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother." Catholic tradition hears each disciple standing in that place. Carmelites took it personally: the order has long called Mary its mother and patroness, and the brown scapular this path met earlier is worn as a sign of belonging to her. Second, sister. This is the surprising one. A sister isn't above you. She's beside you, walking the same road. Jesus says, in Matthew: "For whosoever shall do the will of my Father, that is in heaven, he is my brother, and my sister, and my mother." Luke shows Mary doing that will, with her yes to the angel. So Carmelites see her as a fellow disciple, one of them, praying, listening, trusting in the dark. Third, the quiet one. Luke says of her, after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." That is the Carmelite vocation in a sentence. Not many words. A heart that keeps things and turns them over. Teresa, John, Thérèse, Elizabeth: all of them learned that kind of prayer, and Carmel sees Mary as the one who shows them how. Fourth, near, not distant. Thérèse once said, near the end of her life, that Mary is more mother than queen. Not a figure on a pedestal, but someone close enough to talk to plainly. Sister and mother: one who goes beside you, one who holds you.
screen: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.` · `A SISTER WALKS BESIDE YOU.` · `SHE KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.` · then, large: `MORE MOTHER THAN QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet Mary simply. Settle, and breathe. No long prayer, no performance. Just a greeting, the way you'd say hello to someone in the next room. If you pray, you can use the angel's words from Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Say them once, slowly, and then stay quiet, the way Mary kept things in her heart. If you don't pray, you can simply hold the picture of a young woman listening, and keep her company in the silence. The bell holds the time.
Mary in Carmel. The order's mother, who holds them, and their sister, who walks beside them in prayer. Today's word.
Your line: sister and mother. Today, be a sister or brother to someone: don't advise from above, just walk alongside for a while. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Carmelites honor Mary as mother and sister: they keep her feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, some wear the brown scapular, and they greet her with the Hail Mary and with quiet, pondering prayer.

fork.setup: you're a new Carmelite novice. someone asks why you'd call the mother of God your sister. what do you answer?
options: because she walked the same road of faith, doing the Father's will.
because the title mother sounds too formal.
because sister is just a nickname with no meaning.
fork.reveal: Jesus calls whoever does his Father's will his sister. Carmel sees Mary, who said yes to the angel, as a fellow disciple beside them.

trapdoor: what you thought: Carmelites have a devotion to Mary, like other Catholics.
what it means: they call her mother, who holds them, and sister, who walks beside them in prayer and trust.
what a scholar hears: an order named for Mary, John 19:27 read as entrustment, and Matthew 12:50 grounding the title sister in shared discipleship.
